utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No, no. He wasn't -- I can't say that he was or he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Didn't you see a lot of that soldier during the day because you were with him for -- well, I don't know, you tell us how long were you with that soldier for on that day?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: On that day, that soldier took us to that meadow and he didn't return the same day. So I never saw him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So you saw him for maybe half an hour, an hour, two hours?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No. Like I said, I didn't see him again. He took us to that field or meadow and I didn't see him after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm trying to make this point: That isn't it right that he got a good look at you and you got a good look at him. You both saw each other clearly over a period of time?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. During the arrest, or rather whilst we were being captured in the basement. And while he was taking us to that meadow, the field -- like I said, he took us out of the house and after that I didn't see him again at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now just skipping slightly forward, you referred to seeing in a restaurant a person who was pointed out to you as Naser Oric. And you said that he asked, Is that the boy that was arrested? So it's right, isn't it, that he didn't say, Is that the boy I arrested?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No. What I said is that I'd heard when talking to that lady cook -- what he asked was, Is this the boy who was taken prisoner. He never said, Is this the boy that I took prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And he didn't recognise you, did he? He didn't show any signs of recognising you?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, let's -- just going back again to when the soldier protected you from bullets by covering you in a ditch. You then said that your grandmother pleaded with the soldiers to let you go. My question is: At this stage you're miles from your home in Bajina Basta, the village where you'd been -- had fallen. You were a 7-year-old boy. Would it have felt safe for you then to wander off on your own and try to get home?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, to recapitulate, you said something to the effect of they let me go; that's not what happened. My grandmother started crying and asked them to let me go, but this is not what actually happened, if you see what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think there was a mistake in translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me help you, Mr. Jones. At this point your grandmother is pleading with the soldier to let you go. That's what you told us. Now, was it -- did it make sense to let you go? Let you go where? I mean, there was fighting going on. I mean, would you have been safe? Where would you have gone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't say. I do remember that she mentioned a ruin that was just across the road, an old ruin, and something about leaving me there. But this came to nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I'm moving to your arrival in Srebrenica. Now, you've recalled lot of detail about events back then. And so my following questions concern what you recall of seeing in and around the town of Srebrenica, not just when you arrived but for the whole 21 days, I think it was, that you were there. So if I could preface that by asking you: You spent a lot of time on the streets in Srebrenica, didn't you, during your stay?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You wandered around during the day, you didn't have anything to do, and so you walked around, met people, spoke to people. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't really walking around too much, but I did spend time outside. Usually I would go from the restaurant to the prison or from the restaurant to the flat where I stayed with that lady cook for a while. That's where I walked. Once I left the flat alone but I was soon returned because probably it would have been too dangerous for me to walk around on my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You saw the situation on the streets and roads of Srebrenica, didn't you? Did you see a great many people living out on the streets, camping out there, cooking food on the streets. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Not really. I don't believe there were too many people there, at least not that I noticed, too many cars or too many people coming and going, at least to the extent that I did move about the centre of Srebrenica. What I told you was all I noticed. There was a market there on one of the days, and that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I want to show just a very short video clip and just to anticipate if there are any objections from the other side. It's really extremely innocuous. It's a video we saw during the opening speech, and it just shows some street scenes in Srebrenica in early 1993. It's not evidence or anything as such. It's just to see if that will jog the recollection of the witness, whether he will agree that that was what the conditions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had some discussion with Defence counsel this morning prior to the start of the trial today. And just for the record, I have not been given a copy of this video, only a reference in an e-mail that there will be a video shown to this extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's okay then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: May I just ask you a question. What was the distance, as far as you can remember, between this so-called restaurant and the prison? In other words, how many metres do you think you had to walk between the restaurant and the prison? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me see. Maybe 80 to 100 metres. There was just one building in between. You came out of the prison and around the corner was the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And when you went from this restaurant to the prison, did you pass any larger place or market or something like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't pass by the bazaar, but I saw it and I knew where it was; it was slightly further up. I learned later that I was passing by a department store. Then there was the courthouse and just before the courthouse there was another building. I didn't go inside. I didn't know what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If I could just follow that up with a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: How long did it take you to walk from the apartment where you were staying to the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you that now. I read in the year 2000 my statement - and I don't know how it came to be recorded there - that it was a couple of metres. I don't know how it could have come across that way. It wasn't a couple of metres, because that building was behind the market.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So was it a 5-minute walk, 10-minute walk, 20-minute walk?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. When you walked from the apartment where you were staying to the restaurant, roughly how long did that take you?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Let's say 10, 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: During that time you were walking through the streets and you were seeing life around you?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll show you the video and it's very -- I'll just show a few seconds of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If the booth could please play the video and I'll say stop when we need to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just look at that scene, those images, Mr. Mitrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's all right. We don't need the sound. And in fact we can stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, in fact seeing those images, does that reflect a bit of what you saw when you walked the streets in early 1993 in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I did not see scenes like this, nothing like what I saw on the screen now. I probably didn't go around that area. I must have moved in a different area of Srebrenica, because I didn't see scenes like this. I could see people milling about. I could see that bazaar, whatever they were selling there, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let's speak about conversations which you might have had. I'll put it to you that people talk to young children quite naturally. Do you recall any conversations which you had with refugees or other Muslims which they told you about where they'd come from, about what the food situation was, and that sort of thing, any recollections at all?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me see. I think the situation with food wasn't very good like everywhere else during the war. I ate the same food over and over again every day. Myself, and I suppose the others, weren't much better off.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What I'm driving at, Mr. Mitrovic, is that you've told us this morning of recalling specific conversations in the restaurant concerning Naser Oric, and you've told us about very specific events. And so as I mentioned, I'd be testing your memory. Can you tell us of any conversation which you had in the whole time you were in Srebrenica where somebody told you, a Muslim told you, about the conditions of life there? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I could hear people talking, for instance at the apartment where I was staying when people gathered there at night. And I could understand from what they were saying that their life wasn't easy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: How many people were in the apartment, staying in the apartment with you, approximately?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if they were a family, but four or five people were staying in that apartment all the time, and there were more people coming to visit in the evenings.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Were these refugees or were these people from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: That much I don't know. I didn't ask and -- I didn't try to elicit any information from them and I didn't dare to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of any of the people who you stayed with at that apartment -- who were staying at the apartment where you stayed?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't remember the names of the people I met in that apartment. If I had given a statement right after the war, maybe I could have remembered it then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You were at that apartment for more than two weeks, weren't you? Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But in those 21 days most of the time I spent in that apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's what I'm driving at, Mr. Mitrovic, is that you spent a lot of time in that apartment. You spent much less time in the prison, and you spent only a brief time in the restaurant when you told us that Naser Oric was pointed out to you. So I what I'm trying to establish is, is this -- do you have genuine memories of Srebrenica or are you recalling specific events that you've been told to recall?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No. What I remember, I remember really. And as for Mr. Naser Oric, I didn't want to say that it was 100 per cent him. But it is not true that I am saying things that I heard from other people before the war. I'm telling things that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you play with other Muslim children when you were in Srebrenica during those 21 days?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That kind of thing happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of any of your playmates in that time?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you told us you were taken to the SUP and it was put to you a couple of times that you were interrogated. Isn't it correct that you were simply asked some questions, that it wasn't a fierce interrogation lights in your eyes, gestapo-style interrogation, you were simply asked some questions?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It was also put to you -- in fact, it was the Prosecution who said that you were removed pursuant to a military authorisation. You don't actually know, do you, what authorised you to be taken from the SUP to the apartment [Realtime transcript read in error "to/from"], do you?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: That's right. I don't know. It must have been done with somebody's approval, somebody's permission because it couldn't have been possible for me to be taken there without anybody's knowledge or approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may and also be of assistance of my learned friend. In the question as translated or typed out on the monitor, was authorised for you to be taken to the SUP from the apartment. I think it is in reverse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It should be -- thank you, Mr. Wubben, for pointing this out. It should be the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So, in other words, you assumed that someone must have authorised you to be taken from the SUP. You don't know if it's civilian or military or who authorised it?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Right. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned a one-armed man. I think -- was he the one who took you from the SUP?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was he a policeman as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you remember that he was called --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No means what? No, he wasn't a policeman; or no, I don't know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he was not a policeman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, he wasn't in any uniform?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No, he wasn't. And I said so before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was called Zele. Does that name ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember that. I would like to know his name because he treated me decently and everything, but I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you describe him at all apart from the arm? Can you describe his hair, for example, his hair colour?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No. All I know was that he was of medium height, slightly stalky, but I can't remember his hair colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine. How about his age? Did you have some idea of his age?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. He could have been 30, 35. He was middle-aged, let's say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is that something which -- that was your impression at the time as a 7-year-old that you saw this man and he must be between 30 and 35, or is that now looking back you think that he must have been that age?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's probably true that I didn't give it any thought at that time. I didn't look at a person and think how old he was. But when I was giving the statement in 2000, that man was mentioned and I said what I said according to what I remember. I couldn't remember much. I remember that he had only one arm, that he was of medium height, but not much else.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I was going to ask about your 2000 statement, because in that statement - and it's page 6, seventh paragraph - I don't need to refer you to the text but speaking of Mandza you said: "The Muslim soldier called Mandza lived very close to the lady's apartment that I stayed at. I think he was married and had two children. I think that Mandza was about 33 to 34 years old at that time in 1993." Now, I ask about that because I'm not sure if as a 7-year-old one's able to estimate an age that exactly. So that's my question. At the time you saw Mandza, did you think, Ah, he must be around 33 to 34?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No. It was an estimate in response to the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was it suggested to you that he would have been around that age?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean that somebody else suggested it to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, turning to the apartment where you stayed, the woman who -- in whose apartment you stayed was called Bahra, wasn't she? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Now, again that is something that I found out later after I returned from the prison. I learned that the woman's name was Bahra.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you were perfectly well treated the entire time you were in Srebrenica, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, basically. It's true that on one occasion - and I can't tell you exactly at what time it was now - I spent half a day or an entire day with a man who was a bit on the rough side with me. But then that incident in the canteen happened, and I thought the cook must have told Naser that this man was a bit heavy-handed with me. And that's why he said what he said. I mean when he said that nobody must touch me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And leaving that incident aside, would it be fair to say even the people were pretty nice to you when you were in Srebrenica, friendly?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: To me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you were taken to see your grandmother every day that you were in Srebrenica. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, we've spoken about the restaurant where you've said you saw soldiers. Isn't it right that there were also refugees there as well and other civilians?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I did not see civilians in the strict sense of the term, refugees as you put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You saw people not in uniform at the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But they too were probably troops. I used to see them, but not often. I also saw some refugees on occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And for the ones in civilian uniform or civilian clothes, are you saying they had -- they all had weapons with them and that's why they're troops, or are you just speculating?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, some of them had weapons. That's why I say that I cannot really ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you went with the cook Bahra and I think you said with other cooks to the prison with the food. Isn't it right that the food was the same for the guards and the prisoners at the prison?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: There was no big difference between the meals. It was much the same for everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And wasn't the food that was being prepared at the restaurant and taken to the prison, wasn't it pretty much the same as what the people were eating throughout Srebrenica or at least in the apartment where you stayed?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the food that was cooked in the canteen, was it similar to the food I ate at the apartment with the people I was staying with?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was much the same food for everybody. There was not much choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And the men at the prison received two meals a day. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I cannot confirm with any certainty one way or another. They did get two meals a day. I can't say anything about three meals.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It was two that I said. There might have been a mistranslation. Okay. Now, as far as the women are concerned, you saw the women, including your grandmother, every day. They were perfectly well-treated, weren't they, as far as you could see?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And wasn't there a stove in their room to keep -- to ward off the cold and to keep them warm?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a stove.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, as far as the men's cell is concerned, you never actually entered it, did you?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't go inside, but I could look inside from the hallway. I could come really close, a couple of times at least, when breakfast or lunch was distributed to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did the guards stop you from going into the men's cell?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: It all depends -- yes, they did stop me from going inside. But it all depended on who the guard on duty was, what kind of man he was. Sometimes they let me come up really close up to the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Generally did you get the impression that the guards didn't want you to see the men and the condition they were in?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to say now, but I don't think looking back that they wanted to keep me from seeing. But they did not generally let me go there. They didn't even let me get close, except for those occasions when meals were distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's what I'm trying to understand, Mr. Mitrovic, is why the guards would allow you, a 7-year-old boy at the time, to stand and watch while they beat prisoners with sticks for 15 to 20 minutes as you told us. Is that really right, that that occurred?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that really happened. Sometimes I would stay in the prison for as long as one or two hours. I was near the reception room, and from the doorway of the reception room I could see. Not with their explicit permission, of course, but I could see the beatings.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Weren't you horrified at seeing this, and wouldn't that lead you to go to your grandmother and to not stand there and watch what must have been a very disturbing sight?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Right. But while these men were beaten the women's cell wasn't open for me to go in. Sometimes I was left in their safekeeping. And if I hadn't been that young, I would have been even more horrified -- today I would be more horrified than I was then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You said that there were sounds when the -- when the men were being beaten, that they were shouting and screaming. That's something the women would have heard in their cell, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If it was happening every day, then they would have heard it happening every day?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, isn't that speculation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In a way it is I think, Mr. Wubben. I think your objection can only be sustained. Thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, just finally a few last questions. I might be able to finish, actually, fairly soon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you are going to finish very soon, do you have the next witness here or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Apologies. I did say yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know, I know. Would it be practical -- I don't want to force anything on you. Please don't misunderstand me. I know you have certain procedures to follow. But would it be possible to bring the witness here?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: We will find out. We will contact Victims and Witnesses Unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Just a couple of final questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You said that on the day of your exchange Zulfo said to Cana, I think his name is, and perhaps in jest, that because he tried to escape he wouldn't be released. Now, you told us also that Cana was mentally retarded even before his capture. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was a bit like that, but my apologies, I don't think I said if he had escaped. I think he had been out of the prison and then some people brought him back. He did say that, but not quite the way you said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's it. Just to be clear. Cana in fact basically drifted off and was found and was brought back. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but not on that day. That happened before, days previously. I'm not sure exactly, but not on that same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You mentioned how -- I think when you saw him on exchange that he was mentally not well. You're referring -- that was his general state of mind, wasn't it, that he was mentally retarded; that wasn't as a result of any mistreatment as far as you could tell?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did not say that that was a result of mistreatment. He was like that, and that's what he was like when he was brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, finally you mentioned that when you were in Srebrenica you heard I think you said stories, maybe a lot of stories, about Naser Oric. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Quite a lot of stories, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is it right to say that at that time he was something of a legend?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, people were talking about him. My conclusion was that he was some sort of a leader; that was the only conclusion that I could reach, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: He was spoken of with awe and with respect. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. No one ever said anything bad about him, at least not any of the people that I was in touch with at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when you heard all these stories, I take it that you didn't take them all at face value; you would have taken it with a pinch of salt?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course you can't quite understand everything at once. It's difficult to say what is bad and what isn't until things clear up a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So is there re-examination, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Brydensholt, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Brydensholt, who comes from Denmark, would like to put some questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Well, if I go back to your evidence regarding the 13th to the 16th of January in Skelani when you were arrested, did you explain that when you were brought by the man who has arrested you to this meadow or field you passed your neighbours who were having a meal, kind of feast. Could that be true, or was that a misunderstanding?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't walk passed my neighbours. Those people were soldiers, too, wearing camouflage uniforms. I didn't say anything about the feast day. Preparations were underway for a feast day, so there were things to drink and eat there. We just happened to pass them on the way to the meadow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Then when you came to this SUP building, I understand that you were saying that you read on a plaque that it was the police building. Were you able to read when you were 7 years old so that you could --

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I was able to read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Do you remember now how did this shield look like you read?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember the colour. I think it was blue, but I don't think the plaque's around any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the man with the one arm who brought you away from the prison, what did he do? Was he a guard or soldier or have you any idea what was he doing during the day?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. He may as well have been a guard, but he did not wear camouflage uniform. He just came to pick me up and I spent several days with him. I did not see him again after that, but I did not believe that he was actually a soldier bearing all of that in mind and he was missing an arm after all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Yes. Did he also stay in the apartment together with you during those days when you were in this apartment?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Later, no. I spent several nights -- or rather, the next day when he took me to his place, I think. Later on I found out the name was Kazani. It was a small house, but I don't think that's of any importance. I spent the night there. But if you're asking me about later, where I was staying later in that building staying with the lady cook, he was not there if that's what you have in mind. And now that I think about it, I seem to remember that they referred to that person as Zele, as counsel suggested a while ago. It's coming to me gradually. It does ring a bell definitely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Okay. Did you say that you also were taken to the hospital, not only to the prison to visit your grandmother but also to the hospital. What was the purpose of that?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I don't know. I know they took me there. It was a room where some persons were lying. They gave me some tea to drink. I'm not sure what the reason was. They said, This is so that you can tell people that we gave you tea while you were at hospital once you are released, so you can tell others. I'm not sure if that was the real reason for me being brought there or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: You told us about your connection afterwards, after your release with Ilija. What kind of relationship do you have with him? Does he live where you live now? Why is it that you see him and how regularly?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: As for the location of his house, I think he lives across in Serbia in Bajina Basta. But I think he's from Cesici. I think he owns a house there. But he has family in Skelani, so that's why we occasionally meet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Okay. And when you meet where do you meet? Does he come to your home or how are your relationship?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No. It's a friendly relationship. Whenever we meet we say hello to one another, but we're not really that close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: So you don't sit together and you don't have a real opportunity to discuss what occurs when you were in Srebrenica during the war? That's your explanation?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't think he ever came up to me to say anything like that, nor did I for that matter. I have no reason to discuss this with him, if you see what I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: And when you went to the prison to visit your grandmother, you were, I understand, allowed to go into the cell where she was together with the other females. Was the door locked behind you so you were locked up together with them, or could you leave through the door and spend some times outside? You said you were sometimes wandering around in the prison.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The door was opened when meals would be brought in. And the lady cook, sometimes two lady cooks, would stay there until lunchtime was over. I was not kept from coming in as far as those cells were concerned. I was not kept from seeing my grandmother or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: For how long a time -- you say during lunchtime. What would that mean when the door was open? How long a time do you suppose?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, how should I tell? Sometimes I would stay for an hour or two. I would stay there and then afterwards I knew that I would be left with the guards. That was when I could stay a little longer. But whenever I was -- whenever I came to the cell with the lady cooks, I was only able to stay for as long as they were around. But I never tried to return to those cells on my own, therefore I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: What I would be interested to know is: Was the cell door to the ladies' or females' cell, was it locked -- was it locked during lunchtime? Was it locked afterwards?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, locked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Brydensholt. Judge Eser. Judge Eser comes from Germany, and he also would like to put some questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I just have one question with regard to the statement which you gave in July 2000. At that time you have been 15 years old. The statement has been referred to several times, and you have been confronted with certain statements which you made at that time. Now, at the end of the statement in the English version, I read to you: "This statement consisting of a total of nine pages has been read over to me in the Serbian language." Now, you have signed the English version, not the Serbian version. Now, my question is: When this statement was read to you in Serbian, did there already exist a Serbian version? What had been read to you, was it read from an English -- as far as you can recollect from an English paper and translated into Serbian, or do you know whether there already existed a Serbian original?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't quite understand your question, sir. It was probably translated from Serbian into English, the statement that I gave back in the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: We have here your statement in English. There's also a version in Serbian. And there -- the -- my question -- and I wonder that you -- on the one side you signed the English version, but there's no signature on the Serbian version. And so my question: If at the time when this statement was re-read to you was already written in Serbian, why your signature was not put on the Serbian version but rather on the English version?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: The Serbian version, I'm really not sure why it's there. I'm quite unable to understand this myself why the Serbian version was not signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: So it seems as if you have signed something at the end of each page which you have not really read on your own but which was read to you in your own language. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't quite see where you're going. If you could please simplify the question, Your Honour, because I find it very difficult to understand what exactly you're getting at, the very essence of what you're asking me, if you could just please simplify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: This is the case as with almost all statements we have. And perhaps the Prosecutor could explain at one point how this was handled. Just to tell you once more: What we have here is an English version of your statement of 2000 and a version in the Serbian language. And your signature is on the English version and not on the Serbian version. Also you have stated that it was read to you in Serbian. Do you now understand why I am a little bit wondering whether there was -- if there already existed a Serbian version it would have been normal to sign the Serbian version, not the English one.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection back in the year 2000 I did sign the Serbian statement. It was given to me to read and I signed it. That's at least what I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I see that Mr. Wubben would like to enlighten Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. Of course I didn't witness this statement and -- being typed. But the normal practice is indeed that there is an interpreter certified -- who can certify, as you find out on page nine of nine of the interpreter certification, and the practice is that the questions are put in English and then translated in B/C/S, the answer in B/C/S and then translated back into English. And that has as an outcome -- and again this is my experience on questions put forward to projected witnesses. And then finally there is a statement who is -- and then I can refer to the page nine of nine of that English statement in which in the paragraph 3 the interpreter stated: "I have orally translated the above statement from the English language to the Serbian language in the presence of Branimir Mitrovic, who appeared to have heard and understood my translation of the statement." So that's the normal practice, as I can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think that explains it clearly. Now, Mr. Wubben, we're finished basically. If you don't have the other witness coming over, we're finished. Can you inform the Trial Chamber if the witness -- if it's possible to bring the witness after the break or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are in the middle of the proofing of that witness, so we are not in a position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We can -- that is perfectly understandable. It's not a problem with us. We were just trying to make full use of the time allotted to us, but unfortunately we cannot today. So we will need to adjourn. We will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00. I don't know which courtroom. This one, in this claustrophobic Courtroom II. I'm also reminded that it is an important day for our usher. It's her birthday, so on behalf of the Trial Chamber we wish you all the best. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
